construction_notes: Dependent variable: "hours accounted as FTE from salaried employees with academic education in administration or social science etc." (p. 40). The included degree programmes are listed by DISCED-15 code in Appendix A; medicine and psychology are excluded.

"In the article, four independent variables pertaining to revenue are included in the model, all of which are calculated in Danish Kroner (DKK) and converted to US dollars. The fifth variable is equity, and the sixth is organisation age (in years)." (p. 40)
Table 2 note (p. 42): "Independent variable: Sources of revenue in DKK million." The Results text expresses the same unit as $158,000; no conversion was performed by this extraction.
Revenue is coded into four categories by crossing earmarked/non-earmarked with private/public source (Table 1, p. 41).
Equity is included as "a proxy for consolidated organisational stability" (p. 40).

Appendix B (p. 46) gives whole-sample descriptives with a Danish decimal comma: Academic FTEs 5,4 (SD 15,7); Private non-earmarked funding 96,8 (235,5); Public non-earmarked funding 17,9 (69,1); Private project funding 1,3 (4,9); Public projects 15,4 (73,6); Equity 21,3 (66,0); Organisation age 27,5 (20,4).
No deflator, winsorising or trimming rule is stated anywhere in the paper.
The panel is "predominantly balanced" (p. 40); the paper reports no attrition correction.

claims.statement: Across all nationwide Danish voluntary social organisations with published audited accounts over 2012–17, DKK 1 million more private non-earmarked revenue (which the text calls $158,000) is associated with 0.021 more administrative academic FTE — a within-organisation correlation the paper reports as significant at p < 0.001 (Table 2, column ‘All organisations’).

register_source.value: Audited annual accounts of the organisations, coded into the four revenue categories of Table 1. Not a Statistics Denmark register: no register code or variable name is given for the revenue variables.

definition.value: Non-earmarked revenue from private sources (private citizens, companies, foundations etc.) — 'income that the organisation itself determines the use of within its mission statements', e.g. a monthly donation from a private citizen (Table 1, category 1). Taken from the organisations' audited annual accounts, coded into four revenue categories, measured in DKK million per organisation-year (the text converts DKK to US dollars and calls one unit $158,000).

timing.value: Measured per organisation-year over the accounting years 2012–17; contemporaneous with the outcome — the paper states no lag.

outcome.label: Number of hours for administrative staff (with academic background) measured in FTE ("academic FTEs")

register_source.value: UDDA and IDAN (the Education and Employment Register, Statistics Denmark) — education and annual working hours of employees; the paper names no register variable

definition.value: Number of hours for administrative staff with an academic background, measured in full-time equivalents (FTE); 'hours accounted as FTE from salaried employees with academic education in administration or social science etc.' The included degree programmes are listed by DISCED-15 code in Appendix A (e.g. 3520 Political science, 4025 Public and private administration and management); medicine and psychology are excluded. The paper treats it as a proxy for the organisation's transaction costs.

timing.value: Measured per organisation-year over 2012–17, contemporaneously with the revenue variables; the paper states no lag or follow-up horizon.

units.value: administrative academic FTE per DKK million of private non-earmarked revenue (the text calls one unit $158,000)

magnitude.interpretation: an increase of $158,000 in private non-earmarked funding positively correlates with an increase of 0.021 administrative FTE, corresponding to a 2.1 per cent increase

estimand.target_population: All organisations among nationwide voluntary social organisations in Denmark with published audited accounts, 2012–17; the coefficient is a within-organisation partial association, which the paper calls a correlation.

population.description: All organisations: All nationwide voluntary social organisations in Denmark identified in the National Board of Social Services (NBSS) review that published audited accounts, pooled 2012–17 (organisation-years). The organisations were identified from the National Board of Social Services (NBSS) review of nationwide social organisations; the 2017 population was 98 organisations, 90 of which provided accounts (92 per cent).
subgroups_defined: Smallest organisations: total annual revenue in 2017 equal to or below the median of $1.2 million
Largest organisations: total annual revenue in 2017 above the median of $1.2 million
population.selection: Conditioned on being a nationwide (not local or regional) voluntary social organisation in the NBSS review AND on having published audited accounts; only revenue used in Denmark is counted.

identification.source_of_variation: Within-organisation year-to-year variation in the four revenue categories, equity and organisation age over the 2012–17 panel of nationwide Danish voluntary social organisations. No reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument is used; the author's sole claim to identification is the organisation fixed effects plus the longitudinal structure.

key_assumptions.assumption: Organisation fixed effects absorb the unobserved, organisation-specific determinants of administrative academic FTEs, so that the remaining within-organisation year-to-year variation in revenue is unrelated to the error term conditional on the other revenue categories, equity and age.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states only that a fixed-effect model is used 'whereby corrections are made for unobserved effects' (p. 41) and that the coefficients are stable under robust and panel-corrected standard errors and when equity and age are omitted (p. 41). It offers no balance test, placebo or pre-trend evidence.

rhs: Unobserved determinants of administrative academic FTEs

implies_edges.from: Organisation fixed effects

key_assumptions.assumption: The 8 per cent of the population that did not publish accounts is not selected on the dependent variable, so conditioning the sample on having published audited accounts does not bias the estimates.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted, not tested: the revenues of the non-participating organisations were identified from the NBSS review, and the author states there is 'not considered to be' a systematic connection (p. 40). No comparison of the two groups on the dependent variable is reported.

implies_edges.from: Published audited accounts (sample inclusion)

key_assumptions.assumption: Administrative academic FTEs are a valid, if minimalist, measure of the organisation's transaction costs: hours worked by staff with the listed academic degrees stand in for application, negotiation, monitoring and reporting work.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The author concedes 'it is not possible to determine their exact job function based on an employee's educational background' (p. 40) and defends the variable on the grounds that it applies a uniform criterion across organisations and over the whole period. No validation against actual task data is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The relationship between each revenue category (in DKK million) and administrative academic FTEs is linear and additively separable from the other revenue categories, equity and age, with a coefficient common to all organisations in the column.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed by the linear fixed-effects specification; the paper prints no estimating equation and reports no test of linearity or of interactions between revenue types. The only concession to heterogeneity is the split by organisation size into columns 2 and 3.

key_assumptions.assumption: The supply of available funding in a given year does not confound the relation between an organisation's realised revenue and its administrative academic FTEs; the author wanted such an external variable and could not build one.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Explicitly flagged as an unaddressed omission: 'an overview of the supply of possible financing (including both public and private sources) does not exist for the examined period' (p. 40). No proxy is substituted and no year fixed effects are reported.

implies_edges.from: Annual supply of available public and private funding
Annual supply of available public and private funding

threats_discussed: The dependent variable covers only a subset of the organisation's transaction costs, and transaction costs also fall on other actors (p. 40).
An employee's exact job function cannot be determined from educational background, so academic FTEs may miss transaction-cost work done by e.g. psychologists or social workers (p. 40).
No external variable for the annual supply of available funding exists for the period, so it could not be included (p. 40).
8 per cent of the 2017 population did not publish accounts (p. 39–40).
The size sub-models explain little (R2 of 0.14 and 0.25 against 0.57 overall) and individual coefficients are insignificant because n is halved (p. 41).
Bureaucratisation may rise with organisational age rather than with funding (Kramer, 1990), which the author tests by including age (pp. 40, 43).
robustness_checks: Robust and panel-corrected standard errors (Beck & Katz, 1995): "In both cases, the coefficients are stable." (p. 41)
Sensitivity analysis omitting the two internal variables: R2 rises to 0.60 and 0.66 when equity and age are omitted, "whereas the coefficients in the model are stable" (p. 41).
Splitting the overall model into the smallest and largest organisations by the 2017 median revenue of $1.2 million (Table 2, columns 2 and 3, p. 41).
unresolved_confounders: The annual supply of available public and private funding: "an overview of the supply of possible financing (including both public and private sources) does not exist for the examined period" (p. 40).
Sector-level isomorphic pressures, which the author invokes in the conclusion as a separate driver of academic staff growth that the model cannot separate from funding (p. 43).

Reverse causality from administrative academic capacity to fundraising success is not addressed; the paper claims only that longitudinal data give "a better opportunity to investigate causal relationships than cross-sectional studies" (p. 41).

estimation.specification: Single linear fixed-effects regression of administrative academic FTEs on all four revenue categories (DKK million), equity and organisation age, with organisation fixed effects and a constant; estimated separately for all organisations and for the two 2017-revenue size halves. The paper prints no estimating equation and does not number one.

heterogeneity.dimension: Revenue type (ranking of the four revenue coefficients within column 1)
heterogeneity.finding: Private non-earmarked funding has the second-largest coefficient of the four revenue types in the overall model (0.021).

evidence.how: Appendix B is printed with a Danish decimal comma (the correlation cells read '1,00', '0,88', '-0,12'), so 'Ave. 5,4' and 'Std. dev. 15,7' for Academic FTEs are read as 5.4 and 15.7. No rounding or rescaling; notation only.

value.claimed_domain: Nationwide voluntary social organisations in Denmark only. The author states explicitly that the conclusions do not carry to the wider voluntary sector.
boundary_conditions: "As a result of these circumstances, the conclusions cannot be generalised to the entire voluntary sector without considering the necessary caveats." (p. 36)
Local and regional voluntary social organisations are excluded and are often too small for academic administrative staff to measure the burden (p. 36).

"the data used is limited to national voluntary social organisations ... they form only one segment of the many types of voluntary associations in many sectors" (p. 44).

timing.value: Measured per organisation-year over 2012–17, contemporaneously with the revenue variables; the paper states no lag or follow-up horizon.

units.value: administrative academic FTE per additional year of organisation age

magnitude.interpretation: the largest has a positive and significant coefficient of 0.255

estimand.target_population: Largest organisations among nationwide voluntary social organisations in Denmark with published audited accounts, 2012–17; the coefficient is a within-organisation partial association, which the paper calls a correlation.

population.description: Largest organisations: Organisations which, in 2017, had a total annual revenue above the median of $1.2 million, pooled 2012–17 (organisation-years). The organisations were identified from the National Board of Social Services (NBSS) review of nationwide social organisations; the 2017 population was 98 organisations, 90 of which provided accounts (92 per cent).
subgroups_defined: Smallest organisations: total annual revenue in 2017 equal to or below the median of $1.2 million
Largest organisations: total annual revenue in 2017 above the median of $1.2 million
population.selection: Conditioned on being a nationwide (not local or regional) voluntary social organisation in the NBSS review AND on having published audited accounts; only revenue used in Denmark is counted.

identification.source_of_variation: Within-organisation year-to-year variation in the four revenue categories, equity and organisation age over the 2012–17 panel of nationwide Danish voluntary social organisations. No reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument is used; the author's sole claim to identification is the organisation fixed effects plus the longitudinal structure.

key_assumptions.assumption: Organisation fixed effects absorb the unobserved, organisation-specific determinants of administrative academic FTEs, so that the remaining within-organisation year-to-year variation in revenue is unrelated to the error term conditional on the other revenue categories, equity and age.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states only that a fixed-effect model is used 'whereby corrections are made for unobserved effects' (p. 41) and that the coefficients are stable under robust and panel-corrected standard errors and when equity and age are omitted (p. 41). It offers no balance test, placebo or pre-trend evidence.

rhs: Unobserved determinants of administrative academic FTEs

implies_edges.from: Organisation fixed effects

key_assumptions.assumption: The 8 per cent of the population that did not publish accounts is not selected on the dependent variable, so conditioning the sample on having published audited accounts does not bias the estimates.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted, not tested: the revenues of the non-participating organisations were identified from the NBSS review, and the author states there is 'not considered to be' a systematic connection (p. 40). No comparison of the two groups on the dependent variable is reported.

implies_edges.from: Published audited accounts (sample inclusion)

key_assumptions.assumption: Administrative academic FTEs are a valid, if minimalist, measure of the organisation's transaction costs: hours worked by staff with the listed academic degrees stand in for application, negotiation, monitoring and reporting work.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The author concedes 'it is not possible to determine their exact job function based on an employee's educational background' (p. 40) and defends the variable on the grounds that it applies a uniform criterion across organisations and over the whole period. No validation against actual task data is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The relationship between each revenue category (in DKK million) and administrative academic FTEs is linear and additively separable from the other revenue categories, equity and age, with a coefficient common to all organisations in the column.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed by the linear fixed-effects specification; the paper prints no estimating equation and reports no test of linearity or of interactions between revenue types. The only concession to heterogeneity is the split by organisation size into columns 2 and 3.

key_assumptions.assumption: The supply of available funding in a given year does not confound the relation between an organisation's realised revenue and its administrative academic FTEs; the author wanted such an external variable and could not build one.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Explicitly flagged as an unaddressed omission: 'an overview of the supply of possible financing (including both public and private sources) does not exist for the examined period' (p. 40). No proxy is substituted and no year fixed effects are reported.

implies_edges.from: Annual supply of available public and private funding
Annual supply of available public and private funding

threats_discussed: The dependent variable covers only a subset of the organisation's transaction costs, and transaction costs also fall on other actors (p. 40).
An employee's exact job function cannot be determined from educational background, so academic FTEs may miss transaction-cost work done by e.g. psychologists or social workers (p. 40).
No external variable for the annual supply of available funding exists for the period, so it could not be included (p. 40).
8 per cent of the 2017 population did not publish accounts (p. 39–40).
The size sub-models explain little (R2 of 0.14 and 0.25 against 0.57 overall) and individual coefficients are insignificant because n is halved (p. 41).
Bureaucratisation may rise with organisational age rather than with funding (Kramer, 1990), which the author tests by including age (pp. 40, 43).
robustness_checks: Robust and panel-corrected standard errors (Beck & Katz, 1995): "In both cases, the coefficients are stable." (p. 41)
Sensitivity analysis omitting the two internal variables: R2 rises to 0.60 and 0.66 when equity and age are omitted, "whereas the coefficients in the model are stable" (p. 41).
Splitting the overall model into the smallest and largest organisations by the 2017 median revenue of $1.2 million (Table 2, columns 2 and 3, p. 41).
unresolved_confounders: The annual supply of available public and private funding: "an overview of the supply of possible financing (including both public and private sources) does not exist for the examined period" (p. 40).
Sector-level isomorphic pressures, which the author invokes in the conclusion as a separate driver of academic staff growth that the model cannot separate from funding (p. 43).

Reverse causality from administrative academic capacity to fundraising success is not addressed; the paper claims only that longitudinal data give "a better opportunity to investigate causal relationships than cross-sectional studies" (p. 41).

estimator.value: OLS panel regression with organisation fixed effects ("fixed-effect model")

estimation.specification: Single linear fixed-effects regression of administrative academic FTEs on all four revenue categories (DKK million), equity and organisation age, with organisation fixed effects and a constant; estimated separately for all organisations and for the two 2017-revenue size halves. The paper prints no estimating equation and does not number one.

heterogeneity.dimension: Organisation size: total annual revenue in 2017 at or below vs above the median of $1.2 million (Table 2, columns 2 and 3)
heterogeneity.finding: Smallest organisations -0.006 (not significant) vs largest organisations 0.255 (***, p < 0.001) (p. 43)

ambiguities: The paper prints no standard errors, confidence intervals or exact p-values; significance is recorded here from the asterisks and the table note alone.

The paper labels Table 2 a 'Correlation' and never writes a causal estimating equation, yet the hypothesis in Section 2.4 and the Results discussion are phrased causally ('transaction costs', 'impact on administrative costs'). The estimand is recorded as descriptive_gap for that reason.
Clustering and the standard errors actually used in Table 2 are not stated; robust and panel-corrected standard errors are mentioned only as a robustness simulation (p. 41).
The Table 2 note gives revenue in DKK million while the text converts to US dollars and calls one unit $158,000; both are recorded, no conversion was performed here.

value.claimed_domain: Nationwide voluntary social organisations in Denmark only. The author states explicitly that the conclusions do not carry to the wider voluntary sector.
boundary_conditions: "As a result of these circumstances, the conclusions cannot be generalised to the entire voluntary sector without considering the necessary caveats." (p. 36)
Local and regional voluntary social organisations are excluded and are often too small for academic administrative staff to measure the burden (p. 36).
Danish social organisations have a more project-based funding composition and are regulated more closely than cultural and sports organisations (p. 36).
"the data used is limited to national voluntary social organisations ... they form only one segment of the many types of voluntary associations in many sectors" (p. 44).

theory_referenced: Transaction cost economics / new institutional economic theory (Coase, 1937; Williamson, 1985)
Neo-institutional organisational analysis and isomorphism (DiMaggio & Powell, 1991; Meyer & Rowan, 1991)
Kramer's (1990) thesis that bureaucratic capacity expands with organisational age

prior_findings_compared.as_stated: it has been established that there is a positive correlation between organisation age and the extent of academic labour, which international studies have also identified (Kramer, 1994)

anchor_quote.text: No significant correlation can be demonstrated here for the smallest organisations, whereas the largest has a positive and significant coefficient of 0.255.
